# Revelation 15: Verse-by-verse research notes

**Gaps.** I found nothing on this chapter from Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org) or Orthodox (oca.org) sources. I also found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org or catholic.com, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. The Catholic view below comes from the Haydock Catholic Commentary on biblehub. I didn't find any Reformed writer at ligonier.org, monergism.com or thegospelcoalition.org. The older Reformed-leaning voices (Geneva Study Bible, Poole, Matthew Henry) come from biblehub and studylight.

---

**v. 1: Seven angels, the last plagues**
- **Guzik:** Chapter 15 goes back over chapter 14's events in more detail. It doesn't move the story forward, which shows Revelation isn't strictly in time order. The "seven plagues" echo Leviticus 26:21. The word for wrath is *thymos*, a hot, passionate anger, as opposed to *orge*, a settled anger. Guzik says 10 of its 11 New Testament uses are in Revelation. "Completed" means reaching a goal: "God isn't just blowing off steam." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The phrase "another sign" takes us back to chapter 12. John returns to the beginning to trace God's punishments again. Seven stands for how far the plagues reach. They are "last" because they lead into the final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm
- **Ellicott:** "Plagues" points back to Egypt. Unlike the trumpets, they are not warnings calling people to repent. They fall on those who have already hardened themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **Wesley:** God had been very patient with his enemies, and now his wrath goes out to the utmost. Even after these plagues, though, his wrath against other enemies doesn't stop (Rev 20:15). https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/

**Where traditions differ: how the plague series fit together**
- **Precept Austin (dispensational):** "The seals and trumpets and bowls are sequential, not parallel." https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-15-commentary
- **Robertson:** He sees the bowls as parallel with the Seven Seals (ch. Rev 6) and the Seven Trumpets. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/rwp/revelation-15.html?print=yes
- **Haydock (Catholic):** Interpreters range widely. Some read the plagues literally, as events just before the end. Others apply them to disasters that struck pagan Rome, and the commentary says the disagreement shows how uncertain such applications are. A cited view (Pastorini) has the plagues spread across the whole Christian era. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/revelation/15.htm

---

**v. 2: The sea of glass mixed with fire; the conquerors**
- **What the fire means:**
  - Walvoord (quoted by Guzik): it shows judgment coming from God's holiness. Others see the red of the Red Sea, making the chapter an "ultimate Exodus." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
  - Barnes: the glass stands for justice, mixed with wrath. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/15-2.html
  - Wesley: the fire devours the adversaries. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-15.html
  - Maclaren: the scene is Israel at the Red Sea, with Pharaoh as the beast. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/revelation/the-song-of-moses-and-the-lamb.cfm
  - Utley (bible.org) lists several theories: the setting sun, judgment, martyrs' blood, or the Red Sea. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-15-16
- **"On" or "beside" the sea:** Guzik says the Greek *epi* can mean on, over or beside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/ Pulpit and Ellicott both prefer "by," meaning on the shore. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **"Conquered":** Precept Austin notes the Greek literally means "came triumphant out of" the beast. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-15-commentary
- **Harps:** Ellicott says they are called "harps of God" because they truly belong to him, and that God draws music out of lives marked by suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm

**Where traditions differ: who the conquerors are**
- **Guzik (enduringword, which your list files under Pentecostal/charismatic):** They are the tribulation martyrs, described in Revelation 7:9-17. They are not survivors. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
- **Precept Austin:** The text doesn't say they are martyrs, but it is "almost certain." https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-15-commentary
- **Wesley (Methodist):** He reads it as those who gained, "or were gaining," the victory, with more of whom were yet to come. https://biblehub.com/revelation/15.htm
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** The singers are the 144,000 of Israel together with the wider "harvest" of Gentiles. The chosen are taken up before the bowls are poured out, as Noah and Lot were rescued before judgment fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/15-3.htm
- **Kelly:** The fire shows these saints went through a fiery tribulation that the elders did not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/15-2.html
- **Wallace (preterist, i.e. fulfilled in the first century):** The beast is the Roman emperor, compared with Pharaoh, and the language points to Nero. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/foy/revelation-15.html
- **Haydock (Catholic):** The sea stands for the storms and persecutions the faithful have come through. The beast stands for idolatry or heresy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/revelation/15.htm

---

**v. 3: The song of Moses and of the Lamb**
- **One song or two?**
  - Guzik: it is one song with two names, joining law and love, Old Covenant and New. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
  - Pulpit: the song of Moses is the song of the Lamb, because the Old and New Testament churches are one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm
  - Barnes: it is a song like Exodus 15, not that exact song. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/15-3.htm
- **Wesley:** It is called the song of Moses partly because it echoes Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32. Mainly, though, Moses represented the Jewish church as Christ represents the whole church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-15.html
- **Ellicott:** Israel watched the fall of the great world power of its day. These saints celebrate the doom of the great world powers "of every age." He stresses that God's righteousness, not just his greatness, is what draws out the praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **Spurgeon:** The song praises God and no one else. Moses says nothing about himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/15-3.html
- **Barclay:** The song is almost entirely made of Old Testament quotations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-15.html
- **Historicist reading (Gill):** Gill makes Pharaoh the very picture of the pope of Rome. Leaving Egypt pictures God's people being freed from the antichrist's bondage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/15-3.htm
- **Text question (scholarly):** The KJV's "King of saints" has no Greek manuscript support. Erasmus put it in. The real readings are "King of the nations" (best attested) and "King of the ages." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm Ellicott prefers "nations," echoing Jeremiah 10:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm Haydock (Catholic) follows the Vulgate's "King of ages." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/revelation/15.htm

---

**v. 4: "All nations will come and worship"**
- **Pulpit:** The word for "holy" here is *hosios*, not the usual *hagios*. The verse gives three reasons to fear God: his holy nature, his rule over all nations, and his now-visible righteous acts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm
- **Ellicott:** *Hosios* points to God doing right as Judge. The song speaks of things still to come as if already done, because they are certain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Holiness means God's uniqueness as well as his purity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-15-commentary
- **Guzik:** Every line is "Your… You…". The singers are focused on God, not on their own victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/

**Where traditions differ: what "all nations" means**
- **Wesley (Methodist):** This is a glorious testimony of the future conversion of all the heathens. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/15.htm
- **Pulpit:** The future tense shows the scene comes before the world's conversion is complete. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-15.html
- **Precept Austin (dispensational):** The judgments remove everyone who refuses God. The rest, seeing his power, believe and are saved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-15-commentary
- **Coffman:** Rist objected that the verse clashes with the rest of the book, which says the nations refuse to repent. Coffman answers that it means the countless redeemed "from every nation." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/revelation-15.html
- **The same studylight page also gives a darker reading:** in the end everyone will fear God, but for unbelievers it will be too little and too late. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/revelation-15.html

---

**v. 5: The temple, the tabernacle of the Testimony, opened**
- **Guzik:** The earthly tabernacle was copied from a heavenly pattern (Exodus 25; Hebrews 8:5). This is the heavenly original. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
- **Pulpit:** The word is *naos*, the inner shrine that held the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm
- **Ellicott:** It is called the tabernacle "of witness" because the ark held God's Law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **Wesley:** This is the holiest place, opening a new theatre for the coming forth of the judgments of God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-15.html

---

**v. 6: The angels' clothing**
- **Guzik:** The angels come from God's presence and act on his authority. Their clean clothes show that his judgment is pure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
- **Wesley:** They are dressed like the high priest entering the most holy place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/15.htm
- **Ellicott:** Their clothes resemble Christ's in 1:13. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **Haydock (Catholic):** Their clothes allude to priestly dress. Good angels can serve God's justice, because justice belongs to God as much as mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/revelation/15.htm
- **Text question:** Some manuscripts read "stone" instead of "linen," and the Pulpit Commentary leans toward "stone." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm

---

**v. 7: Golden bowls from a living creature**
- **Shape of the bowls:**
  - Guzik: they are broad, shallow bowls used in temple worship, so they empty quickly and completely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-15/
  - Wesley: the Greek word means vessels wider at the top than the bottom. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-15.html
- **The living creature as giver:**
  - Pulpit: the living creatures stand for life on earth, which makes them fitting carriers of plagues meant for people. It compares Ezekiel 10:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm
  - Ellicott: God's wrath is simply his righteous law working against sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **"Who lives forever and ever":**
  - Wesley: this adds greatly to how dreadful the wrath is. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-15.html
  - Utley: the phrase rests on the meaning of God's name, YHWH. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-15-16

---

**v. 8: Smoke fills the temple; no one can enter**
- **Pulpit:** The smoke means three things: God's presence and glory, God at work (Sinai), and judgment. As at Sinai, no one may come near while he judges. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/15.htm
- **Wesley:** God's glory cloud protected Israel, yet it also appeared when Korah was judged. So it can signal judgment as well as favour. The plagues followed one another quickly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/15.htm
- **Ellicott:** He compares Exodus 40, 1 Kings 8 and especially Isaiah 6, and concludes that the time for warnings is over. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/15.htm
- **Haydock (Catholic):** The smoke is like that at Solomon's temple and shows God's majesty and power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/revelation/15.htm

**Where readings differ: is the door of mercy shut?**
- **Precept Austin:** God may seal heaven's doors at this point, so no more souls are saved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-15-commentary
- **MacArthur (gty.org, Baptist):** the temple of God which always meant mercy and forgiveness and sacrifice and atonement is now shut. https://www.gty.org/sermons/66-56/the-seven-bowl-judgments-part-1
- **Copeland:** He suggests, more tentatively, that God's patience is over. https://www.ccel.org/contrib/exec_outlines/rev/rev_15.htm
